summary: Registers the MIME type image/tiff so that TIFF images can be labeled properly in email and other MIME-aware protocols. It was a standards-track document and was replaced by RFC 3302.

eli5.summary: Every file sent in email needs a name tag saying what kind of thing it is. This memo creates the name tag for TIFF pictures.

questions: how to register tiff mime type
subtitle: The standard MIME type for TIFF images sent over email and web protocols.

tldr.problem: Email and web applications need a standard label to identify TIFF image files so recipients know how to handle them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the MIME type image/tiff, which applies the standard TIFF 6.0 format specification to Internet messaging and adds an optional parameter to identify variant subsets.
tldr.outcome: The image/tiff type became the standard way to mark TIFF images in email and HTTP, though it was superseded by RFC 3302 which refined the definition.

today: RFC 2302 registered image/tiff as a Proposed Standard but was superseded by RFC 3302, which refined the definition. The MIME type image/tiff remains the standard way to identify TIFF images in email and web protocols.

sections.title: What TIFF Is
sections.content:
TIFF stands for Tag Image File Format, and it is a way to store pictures from scanners, cameras, and graphics programs. The RFC registers the MIME type image/tiff so that email systems, web browsers, and other programs can recognize and handle TIFF files correctly.

TIFF is not a compression standard or a printer language; it is a format for storing raster image data, meaning pictures made up of a grid of pixels. A primary goal of TIFF is to let different applications exchange image data while taking advantage of different scanner and camera capabilities.
sections.eli5: TIFF is a container format for pictures. It can hold simple black-and-white scanned documents or complex color photos. The RFC gives it an official Internet name so mail programs know what to do with TIFF files.

sections.title: TIFF Capabilities
sections.content:
The TIFF 6.0 specification defines several key features. TIFF can describe bilevel images (black and white), grayscale, palette-color (limited color palette), and full-color image data in multiple color spaces.

TIFF includes multiple compression schemes that let developers choose the best trade-off between file size and speed. The format is also extensible and can evolve gracefully as new needs arise. Applications can store unlimited private or special-purpose information within a TIFF file, making it flexible for specialized uses like fax transmission or medical imaging.
sections.eli5: TIFF can store simple black-and-white pictures or detailed color photos. It has several ways to squeeze the picture into a smaller file without losing detail. Different programs can also add their own special information inside a TIFF file.

sections.title: The MIME Registration
sections.content:
This RFC re-defines the image/tiff MIME type to refer to all TIFF 6.0 encoded image data and profiles built on it, consistent with how Internet applications use TIFF in practice. The definition improves on an earlier registration in RFC 1528.

The RFC defines an optional application parameter that a sender can include to identify a specific TIFF variant or subset. For example, a message could specify Content-Type: image/tiff; application=foo to identify the particular TIFF application the image uses. When the parameter is absent, the image is assumed to be baseline TIFF or does not require special handling.
sections.eli5: The official label for TIFF pictures in email is image/tiff. Senders can optionally add a note saying which variant of TIFF the picture uses, but this is not required.

sections.title: IANA Registration Parameters
sections.content:
The IANA registration specifies that no parameters are required to use image/tiff. The optional application parameter is defined for cases where identifying a specific TIFF variant is useful. The RFC notes that new application parameter values should be defined in standards-track RFCs and registered with IANA.

The MIME entity uses binary or Base-64 encoding. Security considerations note that TIFF has an extensible structure, but the fields defined in TIFF 6.0 are descriptive and do not induce processing actions on the recipient.

The registration specifies the magic numbers that identify TIFF files: II 49 49 42 00 for little-endian and MM 4D 4D 00 42 for big-endian encodings.
sections.eli5: Email and web systems can use image/tiff without any special settings. The MIME registration explains how to send TIFF data, how to identify what variant a file uses, and how to recognize TIFF files by looking at their first few bytes.

sections.title: Status and Successors
sections.content:
This RFC refined the earlier TIFF MIME type registration from RFC 1528, which had referred only to TIFF Class F (a subset used for fax). RFC 2302 expanded the definition to cover all TIFF 6.0 profiles and extensions, matching real-world use.

RFC 2302 also references related RFCs from the Internet Fax Working Group: RFC 2301 on Internet Fax file format and RFC 2306 on the TIFF Profile for Facsimile. The registration is part of the MIME specification ecosystem (RFC 2045 covers MIME format and RFC 2048 covers registration procedures).
sections.eli5: An earlier memo (RFC 1528) had created a TIFF label only for fax pictures. This RFC made the label work for all kinds of TIFF pictures, not just faxes. Related RFCs handle how to send faxes and special versions of TIFF.
